name: Times club monthly special crossword No 275

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Recalled emotional problem but not an antique that reeks

definitions.note: an old interjection voicing disgust at a smell, defined by what it is used for

indicators.note: 'not' tells you the following letters are to be left out of the word
to recall is to call back, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a hang-up is a neurotic emotional difficulty
taken as written, and removed

explanation.surface: Someone digs up an old emotional hang-up while rejecting a smelly antique.
explanation.walkthrough: HANGUP loses AN to leave HGUP, which read backwards is PUGH. The definition is a description, not a synonym: an archaic exclamation used of something that stinks.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers lists the word as an obsolete interjection expressing disgust, a forerunner of pooh, the noise made at a bad smell.

clue.text: Dice bananas to feed punctilious person who’ll see to plates

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for the person, completed by 'person' in the wordplay

indicators.note: to go bananas is to go crazy, so these letters are scrambled
food goes into a mouth, so one piece is placed inside the other

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
a purist insists on strict correctness

explanation.surface: A fussy cook chops bananas into dice before serving the plates.
explanation.walkthrough: Plates are feet, from the Cockney rhyming slang 'plates of meat'; the kitchen picture of dicing and plating is the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: A chiropodist-like specialist who trims toenails and treats corns cares for feet, which rhyming slang calls plates.

clue.text: Husband drops in suddenly to stop contact with red meat

indicators.note: in a down entry, something that drops leaves its place and falls lower
'in' says the letter is set back inside the remaining word

blocks.note: H is the standard abbreviation for husband
to ghost someone is to end all contact abruptly and without explanation

explanation.surface: A husband pops in without warning, ending a lover's tryst over a steak.
explanation.walkthrough: In GHOST the H falls two places down the column to sit before the T. Gosht is the Urdu and Hindi word for meat, usually mutton or goat, familiar from curry-house menus.
explanation.definitionFit: On South Asian menus the word names mutton, lamb or goat, which counts as red meat, as in rogan gosht.

clue.text: Something to chew bearing downy coat: almost 50 per cent is primarily cudweed

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word loses its last letter
primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter is wanted
to bear is to carry, so the outer word carries the rest within it

blocks.note: chewing gum
nap is the soft raised pile on cloth
fifty per cent is a half; it loses its last letter
the first letter of 'is'

explanation.surface: A note on a chewable plant with a fluffy coat, half of which turns out to be cudweed.
explanation.walkthrough: GUM holds NAP, HAL and I in turn. 'Something to chew' and 'cudweed' (cud being chewed) make a ruminant picture that hides the botany.
explanation.definitionFit: Gnaphalium is the botanical genus of the woolly-leaved composite plants commonly called cudweeds.

clue.text: Maybe Reitman upset Hollywood actor that can be directed

indicators.note: in a down entry, upset means turned upside down, so the letters read upwards

blocks.note: Ivan Reitman directed Ghostbusters; 'maybe' because other Reitmans exist
Clark Gable, star of Gone with the Wind

explanation.surface: A director annoys a Hollywood star who is easy to direct.
explanation.walkthrough: The film-set picture suggests 'directed' means by a film director; here it is steering. Reitman is defined by example, with 'Maybe' flagging his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: A navigable river or craft is one that can be steered or sailed along, so it can be guided.

clue.text: Mark to enter round ahead of seeing that standing

indicators.note: standing means upright, so in a down entry the letters read from the bottom up

blocks.note: pre- means before
as in 'as you're here', meaning since

explanation.surface: A note about the mark that tells a standing singer when to come in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' is not a boxing round or a circle but a musical round, a canon. The surface makes 'standing' sound literal; it turns the short word over.
explanation.definitionFit: In a musical canon or round, this symbol shows each successive voice the point at which it should come in.

clue.text: Military in early hours supported unlimited form of hybrid combat

definitions.note: a phrase meaning the armed forces' word for the morning

indicators.note: without limits means without its boundaries, so the outer letters go

blocks.note: backed means supported; it loses both ends
mixed martial arts, which blends several fighting styles

explanation.surface: Soldiers in the small hours backing an all-out kind of mixed fighting.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase comes from the old British signallers' alphabet, where A was Ack and M was Emma, so a.m. was spoken this way.
explanation.definitionFit: Forces signalese spelled out a.m. using the phonetic letters for A and M, so it means in the morning.

clue.text: Prevent electronic chip in Trident failing

indicators.note: something failing is going wrong, so these letters fall into disorder

blocks.note: an IC, an integrated circuit, is an electronic chip
taken as written

explanation.surface: Stop a dodgy chip inside a Trident missile from failing.
explanation.walkthrough: Trident is Britain's submarine-launched nuclear missile system, which makes the electronic chip sound like hardware. 'Electronic' qualifies chip, not a separate E.
explanation.definitionFit: To interdict is to prohibit or forbid, or to block an enemy's movement, both ways of stopping something happening.

clue.text: A gazelle, a second, then 3600 of them

blocks.note: a mo is a moment, a second
3600 seconds make an hour, abbreviated HR

explanation.surface: A gazelle timed over a second, then over an hour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of them' refers back to seconds, so 3600 seconds is one hour.
explanation.definitionFit: The mohr is a large West African gazelle, the dama gazelle, named in Chambers under this spelling.

clue.text: Homer’s contemporary leads for initial Simpsons episode, with his annoyed grunt wrapping up

indicators.note: leads are the front runners, so the first letters of the next words are taken
to wrap is to enclose, so one piece goes around the other
in a down entry, up means the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: Homer Simpson's catchphrase D'oh!
the first letters of these three words

explanation.surface: Homer Simpson grunts his way through the first episode of the show.
explanation.walkthrough: The Simpsons cartoon is the false trail: 'Homer' is the Greek poet, though 'his annoyed grunt' borrows Homer Simpson's catchphrase. The initials go between its last two letters before everything reads upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Hesiod, author of Works and Days and the Theogony, was a Greek poet active around the same era as the epic poet.

clue.text: From sister in France, taking against English jobless?

indicators.note: to take in is to receive, so one word holds another

blocks.note: de is French for from, carried by 'in France'
soeur is French for sister
v for versus
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Asks whether a French nun turned against England has lost her job.
explanation.walkthrough: SOEUR takes V inside before its R. The answer is a French borrowing meaning idle or with nothing to do.
explanation.definitionFit: The borrowed French adjective describes someone unoccupied and at a loose end, with no work to do.

clue.text: Tough leaves rear of High Court and Britain in turn

indicators.note: the rear of a word is its back end, so only its final letter counts
to turn is to face the other way, so the whole string runs backwards

blocks.note: its last letter
CT is the abbreviation for court
the United Kingdom

explanation.surface: A tough character walks out on the High Court and Britain in turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tough' looks like a person, the thug who leaves; with 'leaves' it is the definition. The word means a packet of strong vellum sheets used by gold-beaters.
explanation.definitionFit: Gold-beaters hammer gold between sheets of hard-wearing vellum, and the bundle of these durable sheets is given this name.

clue.text: Perhaps a tiny old Burmese knife to remove limbs

blocks.note: first meaning: an old word for a kitten, a Burmese being one breed
second meaning: a long double-edged surgical knife for amputations

explanation.surface: A small antique Burmese dagger used to hack off limbs.
explanation.walkthrough: Burmese looks like a person or object from Myanmar, so a 'Burmese knife' reads as one thing; Burmese is a cat breed and the knife is separate.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an archaic diminutive meaning little cat, and also names the slender amputating blade once used by surgeons.

clue.text: Oz writer’s heading to last lines to be safe

indicators.note: the heading is the front letter, sent to the last place in the word

blocks.note: L. Frank Baum wrote The Wonderful Wizard of Oz
RY is the abbreviation for railway lines

explanation.surface: An Australian author's guidance about the final lines, written to play it safe.
explanation.walkthrough: Oz looks like Australia; it is the land of Oz. 'Safe' is a noun, a place for keeping things, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: An aumbry is a recess or locked cupboard, often in a church wall for sacred vessels, a secure store.

clue.text: Burn out, just retaining kinetic energy without interruption

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or disordered, so these letters are scrambled
to retain is to keep hold of, so one word holds the other

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
just as in merely
KE is the physics abbreviation for kinetic energy

explanation.surface: A physics note: a fire burns out, keeping up its energy without pause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Burn out' suggests exhaustion, but 'out' is the signal to rearrange. The energy sits just after the first letter of the four-letter word for 'just'.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something in an unbroken way means continuously, with no pause or break in the sequence.

clue.text: A train outbound circuitously skirts old hedging

indicators.note: a circuitous route wanders about, so these letters go round in a new order
to skirt is to go around the edge, so the scrambled letters surround another

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A departing train takes a winding route around an ancient hedge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outbound' looks like describing the train but is part of the letters; 'hedging' is not a garden hedge but evasive talk.
explanation.definitionFit: A jocular word for talking around a subject, being evasive and indirect rather than coming to the point.

clue.text: Wader in northern estuary, not the first time

indicators.note: without its first means the opening letter is dropped

blocks.note: the Humber is the large estuary in north-east England
bird is British slang for a prison sentence, from rhyming slang bird-lime

explanation.surface: A wading bird sighted on a northern estuary, though not for the first time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not the first time' reads as one phrase, but it splits: 'not the first' acts on the estuary and 'time' is a prison stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: This is another name for the hammerkop or umbrette, an African bird of the stork family that feeds in shallow water.

clue.text: Taking place, though for the first time, delivers elevators

indicators.note: 'for' means instead of, so new letters swap in where the earliest T stood

blocks.note: PL is the abbreviation for place
as in 'clever, if lazy'
to utter a speech is to deliver it

explanation.surface: Something happening for the very first time brings in the lifts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking place' looks like one phrase meaning happening, but the words split. 'Time' is T, and only the first of the two Ts in the word for 'delivers' is swapped out.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are agent nouns for things or people that raise something up, so they mean the same.

clue.text: On vessel home, order one private to reverse incompletely understood implication

indicators.note: incomplete means missing a part, so the word loses its last letter

blocks.note: a submarine
being in means being at home
to tell someone to do something is to order them
the Roman numeral for one
a GI is an American private soldier
to reverse is to turn back

explanation.surface: On a ship heading home, a private is ordered to turn back and half understands why.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin word means 'it is understood beneath', used for something implied but not stated. The naval and army words supply the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin term names something left unsaid but taken as read, an implied meaning beneath the stated words.

clue.text: It’s no good on top of extinct volcano, mostly, for NZ lizard

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is cut

blocks.note: NG is the abbreviation for no good
Mount Ararat in Turkey is a dormant or extinct volcano

explanation.surface: Being on top of an old volcano is mostly useless for a New Zealand lizard.
explanation.walkthrough: Mount Ararat in Turkey is the volcano, best known as where Noah's Ark came to rest. 'On top of' places the first piece above the second in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: In New Zealand the Maori name is used for a small reptile, a gecko or skink, so it is a native lizard.

clue.text: Cycled, requiring muscular part of leg

indicators.note: letters that have cycled have gone round, the last coming to the front

blocks.note: asking for something means requiring it

explanation.surface: Cycling demands strong muscles in the leg.
explanation.walkthrough: The cyclist picture hides the move: the final G of ASKING comes round to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: On a horse, this is the muscular upper hind leg between stifle and hock, the equivalent of a calf.

clue.text: Adjutant’s augmented reality celebration

blocks.note: AR is the standard abbreviation for augmented reality
a gala is a festive occasion

explanation.surface: An army adjutant throws a party in virtual reality.
explanation.walkthrough: Adjutant looks like the military officer; it is the adjutant stork, and the 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the Indian name for the adjutant stork, a large carrion-eating bird of South Asia.

clue.text: Tart filled with large seabird

indicators.note: a thing filled with something holds it inside

blocks.note: tart and acid both mean sour
L is the abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A pastry case stuffed with a big seabird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tart' looks like a pastry; it is the adjective meaning sour.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of the auk family, such as puffins, guillemots and razorbills, are ocean-going birds known by this family name.

clue.text: Field officer’s excellent prospect in New Zealand

blocks.note: FO for field officer, plus the 's
sick is slang for excellent

explanation.surface: An army field officer's promising career prospects in New Zealand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prospect' looks like a noun, a chance of success; it is the verb, to search for gold.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australian and New Zealand usage the verb means to search for gold by picking over old workings or rummage about.

clue.text: Discharge angelic order when one has ascended

indicators.note: in a down entry, ascending means leaving a lower place to rise higher

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
the choirs are the ranks or orders of angels

explanation.surface: An angel is discharged from its order once it has gone up to heaven.
explanation.walkthrough: The I of CHOIR moves from the bottom to the top of the column. 'Discharge' is a noun here, a fluid oozing from a wound.
explanation.definitionFit: Besides the blood of the Greek gods, the word means a thin watery fluid seeping from a wound or ulcer.

clue.text: Sanction former pupil over snitch

indicators.note: turned over means upside down, so the letters read upwards in this down entry

blocks.note: to OK something is to sanction it
an OB is an old boy of a school

explanation.surface: Punishing an old boy for telling tales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snitch' looks like an informer; it is old slang for the nose, and so is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are dated British slang words for the nose, so one stands for the other.

clue.text: Language used in Bhubaneswar formerly, and also Riyadh

indicators.note: read as 'and it is in' the following words, it tells you the answer is sitting among their letters

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A note that one language was spoken in an Indian city and in Saudi Arabia too.
explanation.walkthrough: Bhubaneswar is the capital of Odisha in eastern India; its language was formerly spelt this way, now Odia. Riyadh is a red herring for Arabic.
explanation.definitionFit: This was the older official spelling of Odia, the Indo-Aryan tongue of Odisha state, whose capital is Bhubaneswar.

clue.text: And what have you brought back to divert ancient city?

indicators.note: something brought back returns the way it came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: etc, et cetera, means and so on
to siphon off funds is to divert them

explanation.surface: Someone asks what souvenirs a traveller has brought back to amuse an ancient city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And what have you' sounds like a question; it is the phrase meaning et cetera. 'Divert' means redirect, not amuse.
explanation.definitionFit: Ctesiphon was the Parthian and Sasanian capital on the Tigris, near modern Baghdad, now ruins.

clue.text: Mild-mannered, half-lost, so I’d affected primness

indicators.note: with half lost, only one half of the hyphenated word survives
affected means altered or acted upon, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the first six of its twelve letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gentle person, half gone, admits a prim pose was put on.
explanation.walkthrough: Mild-mannered has twelve letters, so half is MILDMA. 'Affected' looks like describing primness, but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes the fussy, prudish, over-fastidious manner stereotypically attributed to a spinster, so it means prudishness.

clue.text: Without emotion, protecting European rodent’s nest

indicators.note: to protect is to shield all round, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: a dry manner is unemotional
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: Coolly guarding a European rodent's home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'European rodent' reads as one phrase, but European is the E and rodent belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A drey is the twiggy nest that a squirrel builds high in a tree.
